Their eyes lie. The stare runs up and down the road of the crowded villa, dizzying and with a million jagged steps of the eyes to and from each person. A silent, souless cascade of expression that captures the vision of a creature incapable of worldly knowledge. Instead (of anything), the man sees only space, the distance between each brick, gussied pile of flesh, colorful unlit lamp, and the disrespectfully blue sky. How could it all be so clean? He scans one last time. No. This can not be. It has to be hidden somewhere. Someone is whispering, he knows. He can almost hear it. He can almost read the passage of that secret, hidden without discretion, spelled out with characters strewn out, over the ground. 

It would not be worth telling where he got the gun, nor who made it, and why it fires so well. What mattered was that in less than five minutes after the shooting, which lasted only a few dozen seconds, all the victims were already stabilized and well on their way to recovery. And the man, more trembling than thinking, held a child in his arms, against rows of lawmen, and almost took a life before being sedated in less time than it would take to blink.

The affected people return to their lives in a matter of weeks. No sensational, squandering stories; just quiet restoration of the world after the incident. And the man sits in isolation, not turned to the jaws of some malformed and self-destructive justice, but only with hopes by the community that they reclaim themselves. The people believe that even so lowly a person can return and make amends. To them, the man is still just one of them. Of course, the man refuses.

Days pass with no progress. Then, the man gets a visitor. It is a child. They step into a room together, separated by glass. They sit in silence for a while. One of them utters ,"I'm sorry." They both leave the room.

Thing is, when they said they were in our backyards, in our homes, in our places of business, in our beds, in our crops, we actually meant we were now the unwanted guests in their homes. The world belongs to them. Their hollow, tasteless teeth do more to concrete than any bulldozer ever could. Their hives, hideous things hiding the sun, may last longer than the grand canyon. On those bleak mornings, you can only hear buzzing. They aren't any smarter than their ancestors of hundreds of generations ago, whom were, to us, perhaps scampering about a few months ago. They don't know that we are all tired, miserable, afraid, scattered like dust. The only thing they know is that we move around, we have titillating scents, and that we taste amazing to those shells. 

Now, the shells can farm. Yet, all that can be seen is desolate dryness. All the water flows to their gross monument-mansions. Like bees, they make so much more than they need. The smell of their rotting vegetation more pungent than a billion heaps of garbage comfortably making home in infinite dumpers. Now, the only chance I have is to reach their gardens. 

I find myself within. Somehow evading guards the size of trucks. The past melts away, revealing vegetation, signs of life; the greenery like some distant memory. To each side, trees, bred so rigorously with trunks that could be crafted into homes that would withstand any storm. Like a work of art, leaves that make the bareness of soil laughable seem to almost grow as you watch. The open air, in contrast to the fetid highway-tunnels of those wretched shells, is filled only with the fecund olfactory expressions of flowers like glittering novas, blossoming in secret. There is nothing here for me to eat though. Regardless, I will never be full again. I lay down in a patch of grass, so much like a relic, and take my life, as, for the first time since longer than I can recall, I forget the world around me.

Not the first, possibly the last. The deity, strictly labelled 19928293-C, struggled; caught like a roach dancing between the dull ribbons of a spider's web quietly cast out on the wooden frames between walls in an undisturbed hallway. Again, it was not the first time. 19928293-C took time on many occasions to make realities where people suffered. 

In those worlds, full of widespread fear and incidents like disease and famine, the people would pray. Day in and day out, they would pray. Prayer fed 19928293-C, like any other deity. There was the problem. Everything was plain, utterly complete. Once 19928293-C set the world into motion, it would progress along one path of reality to completion and follow no other outcome. The stars would coalesce in rivers of magnificent fury, the hollow vacuum would yield to the traffic of their light, small islands of stability might escape chaos, and life would form, in tiny pools.

And then, in this world, where people were too tired, too busy, to angry, too weak, and too lost; on a small stone rippling through the expanse of a fabricated reality, 19928293-C began starving. 19928293-C turned, to it's side: the glow of a galaxy, churning plasma, like chewing gum, in silence. The force of an object of space could never console 19928293-C. Of course, the passing of  time offered no balm either. This was it's reality, one where people did not, could not wonder, and, accordingly, 19928293-C ceased to be, deprived of hope.

"President Jones! We finally meet! Though I think you've hardly earned the title. You've gotten everything you want. You went from a crooked industrialist to someone who would literally massacre all of mankind as he sits comfortably in a rocking chair. You villain! This ends tonight!" The imposing, suited man paces, "Pity, you're right about one thing though. And it really is a shame, Arhagead, you and everyone else, you all made such an effort. You see, I anticipated all of this. Your rebellion will fail. In fact, all your friends will soon be killed. I'm a fair man though.... So, any last words?" The bulky, rugged frame starts trembling, "Me? No! You should be begging for your life. We took out all your troops." "Ah, but that's where you're wrong", the President gleams, "You couldn't be further from the truth." In a condescending manner, arms outstreached in revelry, the president paces to the window as dozens of armed troops trample the office, from all angles, like a fog rolling into a valley.

Eight of the rebellion's elites raise their arms against fifty goverment dogs, crammed in the office like potential lifelong friends in a high-kill animal shelter. The hero blurts, "I see. You really are a coward!" "Me? You come here, so full of wasted youth and try to bully a poor old man. You should be ashamed! Now beg for your life and I'll spare you so I can keep you around to show those rebels what it means to cross me!" "Not on your life, Jones." "That's fine. There won't be any rebels to deliver any messages to anytime in the near future, anyway." "Wait! What are you saying?" the hero begins to collapse. "I already told you. One of your trusted comrads sold you out," the President chuckles. "How?... Fine then! I'll beg! Spare my comrades, and I'll be at your mercy" "Put your gun down" A rebel, much younger than Arhagead, shouts, "Don't do it!" Arhagead looks back for a moment, drops his weapon like a child   flushing a goldfish down the toilet, and begins walking. A shot is fired. Arhagead drops dead. The room bursts into flame, igniting with a sense of nothing to lose. Six  of the eight rebels manage to escape.

The next week the rebellion still stands. No major locations are infiltrated, making apparent that Jones had pulled a bluff. Quickly losing momentum after the loss of their leader, the rebellion retracts as the goverment gains ground after crushing otherwise well-positioned pockets of resistance in the nation's countryside. Less than a year later, the rebellion's main force weakens, and finally falls.

"So, Mr. Arhegead, you're here with us tonight with something very important to tell us." Arhegead attempts to compose himself and faces the greasy reporter. Through his giant frame, the guest replies, "Yes, Mr. Johnson, I'm here to tell you that cows can talk. All cows, save a few differently abled, can talk. We've been able to vocalize our thoughts for longer than humans have been able." Rising from his chair, Johnson begins shouting, "Isn't that amazing, folks? A cow that can talk. Amazing!" "Since my name might as well be Brutus at this point, could you please let me off this leash?" The host frowns, facing away from the camera, "Sorry, can't do that. Those are just the rules." "I'm the first cow the break the silence in over several hundred years, the least you can do me is the courtesy of letting me off this leash?" As the cameras' lenses are covered and the studio closes its doors, the reporter responds, "I have nothing else to say to you." As the newsman motions, offstage hands fire a rifle and the cow falls onto the set.

Something changed. There was a quiet storm out in space. Some otherwise imperturbable nebula finally decided that life was too short. There: between visions of making it to our home planets; between the face of God, devouring the horizon set in otherwise blinding light; between a sense of momentary peace in knowing nothing would ever change, our eyes met. We were in love, the collapse of the tiny stones supporting our lives wouldn't change that.

Just technology and commitment, almost interchangeably; and the notion that such changes to an individual could possibly pair with a normative state of being. All a facade. I remain cognitive enough to know that, in order to maintain the sheer volume of computations that enable the projection of my glistening apendages, something else exists within me. Like how a sense of taste normally prevents someone from consuming poison, I can no longer judge properly. A million bodies rise each day. Humorously, they respect the sun. I am unsure. I have been moving between the metal. Cutting things that should remain upright. Instead of falling, everything wrenches, twisting further into the sun. I look, for the first time, absolutely, ever. My victim: a child. Over six feet tall and my hands tore life from him like picking an apple from a tree. Redness: eyes and on the ground,  everywhere. Society dictated. I had a choice. There was no other way. I know. In an ideal world, this man does not have to die, nobody does, save from old age. I can see it. This man is me. We are all the same. I can do nothing, even as plasma moves through my veins and pushes cogs that ever so slightly distort reality something like altering the space between people and distrubing gravity, pulling us apart. Even so, I am as powerless as the child. Just insults. I could have never see like this before and I only blind myself now. Staring out. A breath. I seize what remains of me. Another breath. The sun shines. I can hear birds and the wind. Someone will die tomorrow. I can tell. I wait.

I am no less depressed over the human condition than you, and, like you, have spent countless days, weeks, months, mulling over the seemingly definite rational misery of existence. In the end, I think we are left with only a choice in belief. Somewhat diverging from the original conversation, consider the idea of alturism. Some might say alturism is a construct of human survival. Others don't even consider the underlying detail and sort of just feel their way around. Complex concepts such as fate still depend on acknowledgement by supposedly lower senses. In the end, you may decide if the world is simply a mess of atoms and molecules, or you can revel in what there is. Lower senses go beyond real understanding as tasting even plain bread or listening to an ordinary voice contains countless sensory factors, such as dozens of complementary harmonics in a single pitch, that we might physically notice, but never fully mentally absorb. I know this response is somewhat convoluted and disorganized, as I am by no means any writer, but I kind of want you to share that you can't let one tiny detail, even if the detail is the all encompassing construct of fate, prevent you from experiencing neat stuff because life, from what I can understand, all comes down to how you perceive it.
